q: Which ancient civilization built the pyramids of Giza?
f: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BCE as a tomb for the pharaoh Khufu.

q: Who was the first President of the United States?
f: Washington served two terms, from 1789 to 1797, and set precedents like the two-term tradition.

q: In what year did Christopher Columbus first reach the Americas?
f: Columbus landed in the Bahamas in October 1492, sailing for Spain.

q: Augustus became the first emperor of which state?
f: Born Octavian, he took the name Augustus in 27 BCE after winning the civil wars that followed Caesar's death.

q: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914 helped trigger which conflict?
f: He was shot in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, and within weeks the great powers were at war.

q: In which year did World War II end?
f: Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan in August and September of that year.

q: Which wall fell in 1989, becoming a symbol of the end of the Cold War?
f: East Germany opened its borders on November 9, 1989, and Germany reunified in 1990.

q: Who was the principal author of the Declaration of Independence?
f: Jefferson drafted it in 1776 as part of the Committee of Five.

q: Which ship carried the Pilgrims to Plymouth in 1620?
f: About 102 passengers made the voyage, and the Mayflower Compact was signed before they landed.

q: Which war was fought between the Union and the Confederacy from 1861 to 1865?
f: It ended with Confederate surrender at Appomattox and the abolition of slavery.

q: Who was Supreme Allied Commander for the D-Day invasion of Normandy?
f: The landings on June 6, 1944 opened the Western Front; Eisenhower later became U.S. president.

q: Which ancient Greek city-state was famous for its militarized society?
f: Spartan boys began military training (the agoge) at around age seven.

q: Which Roman general crossed the Rubicon river in 49 BCE, starting a civil war?
f: Crossing with his army broke Roman law, and the phrase 'crossing the Rubicon' still means a point of no return.

q: Most of the Great Wall of China that survives today was built by which dynasty?
f: The Ming rebuilt and extended the wall mainly in the 1500s and 1600s.

q: Who led Britain as Prime Minister from May 1940 through most of the rest of World War II?
f: Churchill replaced Chamberlain in May 1940 and led until July 1945, then returned in 1951.

q: Which document, sealed in 1215, limited the power of the English king?
f: King John agreed to it at Runnymede, and it became a foundation of the rule of law.

q: Which conqueror founded the Mongol Empire in 1206?
f: At its peak the Mongol Empire became the largest contiguous land empire in history.

q: Which U.S. program landed astronauts on the Moon in 1969?
f: Apollo 11 landed on July 20, 1969, and Apollo 17 was the last crewed lunar mission in 1972.

q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
f: Armstrong stepped onto the surface first; Buzz Aldrin followed about 19 minutes later.

q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
f: It was dedicated in 1886 as a gift marking friendship and the centennial of American independence.

q: Which Egyptian queen allied with Julius Caesar and later Mark Antony?
f: Cleopatra was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt; Egypt became a Roman province after her death in 30 BCE.

q: What was the Black Death?
f: It killed an estimated third or more of Europe's population between about 1347 and 1351.

q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
f: He painted it between 1508 and 1512 for Pope Julius II.

q: Which revolution began in 1789 with the storming of the Bastille?
f: The Bastille fell on July 14, 1789, now celebrated as France's national day.

q: Which country sent the first human into space?
f: Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth in Vostok 1 on April 12, 1961.

q: Which dictator led Nazi Germany from 1933 to 1945?
f: He became chancellor in January 1933 and died by suicide in Berlin in April 1945.

q: Which empire, centered on Constantinople, fell to the Ottomans in 1453?
f: The conquest of Constantinople by Mehmed II ended the eastern Roman Empire.

q: Who led the Soviet Union during most of World War II?
f: Stalin ruled from the mid-1920s until his death in 1953.

q: Which 1919 treaty formally ended World War I with Germany?
f: It imposed reparations and territorial losses on Germany, and many historians link its resentments to later events.

q: Which U.S. president issued the Emancipation Proclamation?
f: It took effect on January 1, 1863, declaring enslaved people in Confederate-held areas free.

q: Which attack drew the United States into World War II in December 1941?
f: Japan struck the U.S. naval base in Hawaii on December 7, 1941.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World stood in Alexandria, Egypt?
f: Built in the 3rd century BCE, it guided ships into Alexandria's harbor for centuries.

q: Who is known as the 'Maid of Orleans'?
f: She helped France lift the siege of Orleans in 1429 and was executed in 1431.

q: Who proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949?
f: He declared it in Beijing on October 1, 1949, after the Communist victory in the civil war.

q: Which civilization built the mountain city of Machu Picchu?
f: The site was built in the mid-1400s and was abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest.

q: Who led India's nonviolent campaign against British rule?
f: His campaigns, like the 1930 Salt March, helped lead to independence in 1947.

q: Which event in 1517 is traditionally said to have launched the Protestant Reformation?
f: Luther's challenge to the sale of indulgences spread quickly thanks to the printing press.

q: Which city was the capital of the Aztec Empire?
f: It stood on an island in Lake Texcoco and fell to Hernan Cortes in 1521; Mexico City now lies on the site.

q: Which 1066 battle led to the Norman conquest of England?
f: William of Normandy defeated King Harold Godwinson and was crowned king on Christmas Day.

q: Who became the first emperor of a unified China in 221 BCE?
f: He standardized writing, weights and measures, and is buried near the Terracotta Army.

q: Which Roman emperor is associated with the 313 Edict of Milan, which tolerated Christianity?
f: Constantine and his co-ruler Licinius issued it; Constantine later founded Constantinople.

q: Which conflict between England and France lasted from 1337 to 1453?
f: It was actually a series of wars, and it ended with France driving the English out of almost all its territory.

q: Which statesman engineered German unification under Prussian leadership in 1871?
f: Bismarck used three wars and careful diplomacy to build the German Empire.

q: Which 1648 settlement ended the Thirty Years' War?
f: It is often cited as the origin of the modern system of sovereign states.

q: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal?
f: He built it in the 1600s as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

q: What did Mikhail Gorbachev's policy of 'glasnost' mean?
f: Glasnost loosened censorship in the late 1980s, while 'perestroika' referred to economic restructuring.

q: Which October 1962 confrontation brought the U.S. and USSR close to nuclear war?
f: It ended when the USSR agreed to remove its missiles from Cuba in exchange for a U.S. pledge not to invade.

q: Who was the leading figure of the early Haitian Revolution?
f: Born into slavery, he led the uprising that culminated in Haiti's independence in 1804.

q: Whose expedition completed the first circumnavigation of the Earth (1519-1522)?
f: Magellan died in the Philippines in 1521, and Juan Sebastian Elcano finished the voyage.

q: Which Mongol ruler founded the Yuan dynasty in China?
f: He completed the conquest of Song China in 1279 and made Beijing his capital.

q: Which 1803 Supreme Court case established judicial review?
f: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote that courts may strike down laws that violate the Constitution.

q: What was the Marshall Plan?
a: U.S. aid to rebuild Western Europe after World War II
w: A military alliance of Western nations
A treaty ending the Korean War
f: Announced in 1947, it sent about 13 billion dollars in aid and helped economies recover.

q: Which Greek city-state is regarded as the birthplace of democracy?
f: Reforms around 508 BCE under Cleisthenes created an early form of citizen assembly rule.

q: Who was the last Tsar of Russia?
f: He abdicated in March 1917 and was executed with his family in 1918.

q: Which Muslim leader recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187?
f: He won the Battle of Hattin and then took Jerusalem, prompting the Third Crusade.

q: Which explorer reached India by sea around Africa in 1498?
f: He arrived at Calicut, opening a direct sea route from Europe to Asia.

q: In which year did the Bolsheviks take power in Russia?
f: They seized power in the October Revolution (November by the modern calendar).

q: Who was the first Chancellor of West Germany?
f: He served from 1949 to 1963 and tied West Germany closely to the West.

q: Which Spanish conquistador led the conquest of the Aztec Empire?
f: Allied with Indigenous rivals of the Aztecs, he took Tenochtitlan in 1521.

q: Which 1814-1815 gathering redrew Europe's map after Napoleon's defeat?
f: Led by figures like Metternich, it aimed to restore a balance of power.

q: What was the idea of 'Manifest Destiny' in 19th-century America?
a: That the U.S. was meant to expand across North America
w: That the U.S. should avoid foreign alliances
That Native nations should hold land in common
f: The phrase, coined in 1845, was used to justify westward expansion.

q: Which people wrote in cuneiform in ancient Mesopotamia and are credited with early writing?
f: Cuneiform began as accounting marks around 3400 BCE in cities like Uruk.

q: Which pharaoh's nearly intact tomb was discovered by Howard Carter in 1922?
f: The boy king's tomb in the Valley of the Kings held thousands of artifacts.

q: Which two countries emerged from the 1947 partition of British India?
f: Partition caused mass migration and violence, and Bangladesh only became independent in 1971.

q: Which war ended with the 1953 armistice signed at Panmunjom?
f: The armistice created the demilitarized zone, and no formal peace treaty was ever signed.

q: Which Carthaginian general famously crossed the Alps with war elephants?
f: He invaded Italy in 218 BCE during the Second Punic War and won at Cannae.

q: Which French emperor died in exile on Saint Helena in 1821?
f: Britain sent him to the remote South Atlantic island after Waterloo.

q: What was the main goal announced for the First Crusade in 1095?
a: Retaking the Holy Land for Christendom
f: Pope Urban II called for it at the Council of Clermont, and Jerusalem fell in 1099.

q: Which Ottoman sultan conquered Constantinople in 1453?
f: He was about 21 and became known as 'the Conqueror'.

q: Which amendment to the U.S. Constitution abolished slavery?
f: It was ratified in December 1865, after the Civil War.

q: Which organization was founded in 1945 to promote international peace and cooperation?
f: Fifty-one countries signed its charter in San Francisco in 1945.

q: Which dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907, with its capital at Chang'an?
f: The Tang era is often seen as a golden age of poetry, trade and cosmopolitan culture.

q: Which 1494 agreement divided newly found lands between Spain and Portugal?
f: It drew a line in the Atlantic, which is why Brazil speaks Portuguese.

q: Which British king ruled during the American Revolution?
f: He reigned from 1760 to 1820, and the colonies declared independence in 1776.

q: Which event is traditionally used to mark the end of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE?
w: The sack of Rome by Alaric
f: The Germanic general Odoacer removed the last Western emperor, a teenager.

q: Which South African leader spent 27 years in prison and became president in 1994?
f: He led the country out of apartheid and shared a Nobel Peace Prize with de Klerk.

q: Which 1815 battle ended Napoleon's rule for good?
f: Wellington and Blucher defeated him in modern Belgium on June 18, 1815.

q: Which 1917 British statement supported a 'national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine?
f: It was a short letter from Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour, and its legacy remains contested.

q: Which country became the first Black-led republic when it declared independence in 1804?
f: Haiti's revolution is the only successful slave uprising to found a state.

q: What were the conflicts between France and the Habsburgs over control of Italy (1494-1559) called?
f: They ended with the Peace of Cateau-Cambresis, leaving Spain dominant in Italy.

q: Which Byzantine emperor built the Hagia Sophia in its current form, completed in 537?
f: It was the world's largest cathedral for nearly a thousand years.

q: The Abbasid Caliphate defeated which empire at the Battle of Talas in 751?
f: The battle is often linked to the spread of papermaking westward.

q: Which ruler of the Mali Empire made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324?
f: He distributed so much gold on the journey that prices in Cairo were said to have been affected.

q: Which 1713 treaty ended the War of the Spanish Succession?
f: It confirmed a Bourbon on the Spanish throne while barring the union of the French and Spanish crowns.

q: Which Roman emperor ruled during the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE?
f: Rumors that he 'fiddled' are myths, but he did blame and persecute Christians afterward.

q: Which Indian emperor embraced Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga War?
f: He spread his moral teachings on pillars and edicts across the Maurya Empire.

q: Which Florentine friar led a puritanical regime and was executed in 1498?
f: His 'Bonfire of the Vanities' burned luxury goods before he fell from favor.

q: What was the 1648-1653 revolt against royal authority in France called?
f: The young Louis XIV's experience of it shaped his drive for absolute monarchy.

q: Which 1868 event ended the Tokugawa shogunate's rule in Japan?
f: Imperial rule was restored, launching rapid modernization.

q: Which 1884-85 conference set rules for European colonization in Africa?
f: No African leaders attended, and it fed the 'Scramble for Africa'.

q: Which 1853-1856 war pitted Russia against Britain, France and the Ottomans?
f: It is remembered for the Charge of the Light Brigade and Florence Nightingale's nursing.

q: Which dynasty was overthrown in China by the Xinhai Revolution of 1911?
f: The last emperor, Puyi, abdicated in early 1912.

q: Which English king was executed by beheading in 1649?
f: He lost the English Civil War, and England briefly became a republic.

q: Which king of Spain sent the Armada against England in 1588?
f: Storms and English tactics wrecked much of the fleet.

q: Which Persian king was defeated by Alexander the Great at Gaugamela in 331 BCE?
f: The victory opened Babylon and the heart of the Persian Empire to Alexander.

q: Who became the first shogun of the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603?
f: His line ruled Japan for over 250 years, until 1868.

q: Which 1919 Chinese protest movement opposed the terms of the Versailles settlement?
f: It began after the Allies agreed to give German holdings in Shandong to Japan.

q: Which reforming brothers were killed in 133 and 121 BCE during the late Roman Republic?
f: Their land reforms provoked violent opposition and are seen as an early sign of the Republic's decline.

q: Which English king defeated Viking forces at Edington in 878?
f: He later organized fortified towns and promoted learning.

q: Who denounced Stalin's crimes in the 1956 'Secret Speech'?
f: He delivered it to the 20th Party Congress, starting the 'de-Stalinization' period.

q: Which event drove the Shah of Iran from power in 1979?
f: It created an Islamic republic under Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

q: Which 1842 treaty ended the First Opium War and ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain?
f: It also opened five Chinese ports to British trade.

q: Which war ended with the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth, mediated by Theodore Roosevelt?
f: Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for the effort.

q: Which 1571 naval battle saw a Holy League fleet defeat the Ottomans?
f: Cervantes, the future author of Don Quixote, was wounded in it.

q: Who founded the Safavid dynasty in Persia in 1501?
f: He made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Persia.

q: Which ruler was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III in the year 800?
f: His coronation on Christmas Day revived the idea of a Western empire.

q: Which city did Rome raze at the end of the Third Punic War in 146 BCE?
f: Rome later refounded the site as a Roman colony.

q: What is the 1932-33 famine in Soviet Ukraine called?
f: It followed forced collectivization and killed millions.

q: Which 1947 U.S. policy pledged support to nations resisting communist takeover?
f: It began with aid to Greece and Turkey and set the tone of Cold War containment.

q: Which 1618 event is considered the spark of the Thirty Years' War?
f: Protestant nobles threw royal officials out of a castle window in Prague.

q: Which Chola king launched a naval expedition against Srivijaya around 1025?
f: It is one of the rare overseas campaigns by an Indian dynasty.

q: Who founded the Askia dynasty of the Songhai Empire in 1493?
f: He expanded Songhai and made Timbuktu a center of Islamic scholarship.

q: Which 1783 treaty formally recognized American independence?
f: Britain also ceded lands east of the Mississippi River.

q: Which Portuguese prince sponsored voyages down the African coast in the 1400s?
f: He rarely sailed himself but sponsored exploration of the African coast.

q: Which Austrian statesman was the dominant figure at the Congress of Vienna?
f: He championed conservatism and a balance of power after Napoleon.

q: Which Mughal emperor promoted religious tolerance under the idea of 'sulh-i-kul' (universal peace)?
f: He ruled from 1556 to 1605 and expanded the empire across northern India.

q: Which admiral led the Ming treasure voyages between 1405 and 1433?
f: His fleets sailed as far as East Africa and were far larger than Columbus's ships.

q: Which pharaoh tried to replace Egypt's gods with worship of the sun disk, the Aten?
f: His successors reversed the change, and his city Amarna was abandoned.

q: Which warlord began Japan's late-16th-century unification before being betrayed in 1582?
f: His work was continued by Hideyoshi and completed by Ieyasu.

q: Which 1948-49 Cold War crisis saw the Western Allies supply a city by air?
f: The Soviets cut off land access to West Berlin, and the airlift lasted about 15 months.

q: Which leader negotiated the 1978 Camp David Accords between Egypt and Israel?
f: Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin signed them, leading to the 1979 peace treaty.

q: Which Chilean president was overthrown in a 1973 military coup?
f: The coup brought General Pinochet to power for 17 years.

q: Which kingdom's all-female warrior corps was known as the Agojie?
f: The Dahomey kingdom is in modern Benin, and the Agojie fought until the French conquest in the 1890s.

q: Which of these was NOT one of the four emperors of the 'Year of the Four Emperors' (69 CE)?
f: The fourth emperor of that year was Vespasian, who founded the Flavian dynasty.

q: Which 1526 battle opened the Ottoman conquest of much of Hungary?
f: Suleiman the Magnificent's victory killed King Louis II of Hungary.

q: Which Ethiopian emperor defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa in 1896?
f: The victory kept Ethiopia independent while almost all of Africa was colonized.

q: Which king of Kongo was baptized in 1491 under the Christian name Joao I?
f: His son Afonso I made Christianity a pillar of the kingdom.

q: Which Mughal emperor regained his throne in 1555 with Safavid help after years in exile?
f: He died within a year, leaving the empire to his son Akbar.

q: Which sisters led a rebellion against Han Chinese rule in Vietnam in 40 CE?
f: They briefly ruled and are celebrated as national heroines in Vietnam.

q: Which 1559 treaty ended the Italian Wars?
f: It left Spain's Habsburgs dominant in Italy.

q: Which Byzantine emperor was captured by the Seljuks at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071?
f: The defeat opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

q: Japan's Kamakura period (1185-1333) is named for what?
f: Minamoto no Yoritomo established the first shogunate at Kamakura.

q: Which Khmer king built Angkor Wat?
f: It was built in the early 1100s as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu.

q: Which 1878 congress revised the Russo-Turkish peace of San Stefano?
f: Bismarck hosted it, acting as an 'honest broker' among the great powers.

q: Which Mongol commander sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate's political power?
f: His campaign was cut short, and the Mamluks later stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut.

q: Which Polish king led the relief of Vienna in 1683?
f: The victory marked a turning point against the Ottoman advance in Europe.

q: Who ruled the Aztec Triple Alliance just before Moctezuma II?
f: He expanded Aztec power and dedicated the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan in 1487.

q: Which of these was NOT one of Rome's 'Five Good Emperors'?
f: The five were Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius; Commodus, Marcus Aurelius's son, was a notorious successor.

q: Which ruler founded the Pagan (Bagan) Empire in Burma in the 11th century?
f: He united Upper Burma and adopted Theravada Buddhism.

q: Which 1260 battle saw the Mamluks halt the Mongol advance in the Middle East?
w: The Battle of the Kalka River
f: The other three were Mongol victories, which makes Ain Jalut stand out.

q: The Congo Free State (1885-1908) was the personal possession of which monarch?
f: Reports of atrocities led Belgium to take it over as a colony in 1908.

q: Which Sasanian king captured the Roman emperor Valerian in 260 CE?
f: It is the only time a Roman emperor was captured alive by a foreign enemy.

q: Which 1521 imperial assembly declared Martin Luther an outlaw?
f: Luther refused to recant before Emperor Charles V.

q: Which Ottoman sultan conquered Mamluk Egypt in 1517?
f: The conquest brought the holy cities of Mecca and Medina under Ottoman control.

q: What principle did the 1555 Peace of Augsburg establish in the Holy Roman Empire?
a: Each ruler chooses the religion (Lutheran or Catholic) of his territory
w: Freedom of worship for all subjects
f: It was later summed up as 'cuius regio, eius religio'.

q: Which silver mountain in modern Bolivia financed much of the Spanish Empire?
f: At its peak in the 1600s, Potosi was among the largest cities in the world.

q: Against which state did Bohdan Khmelnytsky's Cossack uprising of 1648 rise?
f: The uprising reshaped the politics of Eastern Europe and Ukraine.

q: Which Chinese ruler founded a new dynasty called the Zhou in 690, interrupting the Tang?
f: She remains the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right.

q: Which Ghurid ruler defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192?
f: The victory led to the founding of the Delhi Sultanate.

q: With which government did Germany sign the March 1918 Treaty of Brest-Litovsk?
f: Russia gave up huge territories to leave World War I, but lost them back after Germany's defeat.

q: Which Venetian doge led the Fourth Crusade's diversion to Constantinople in 1204?
f: He was reportedly over 90 and blind when he led the fleet.

q: Which Neo-Assyrian king built the great library at Nineveh?
f: His library preserved thousands of cuneiform tablets, including the Epic of Gilgamesh.

q: Which ancient Indian advisor is credited with the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft?
f: He served Chandragupta Maurya, and the book is compared to Machiavelli's 'The Prince'.

q: Which Byzantine emperor earned the nickname 'the Bulgar-Slayer'?
f: He crushed the First Bulgarian Empire in 1018.

q: Which European state was first to legislate a ban on the Atlantic slave trade, in 1792?
f: The ban took effect in 1803, four years before Britain's.

q: Which U.S. Supreme Court ruling in 1857 declared that Black Americans could not be citizens?
f: The decision inflamed sectional tensions before the Civil War.

q: Which 1944 conference set up the post-war international monetary system, including the IMF?
f: It was held in New Hampshire and tied currencies to the U.S. dollar, which was tied to gold.

q: Which Persian king began construction of the ceremonial capital at Persepolis?
f: Construction began around 518 BCE; Alexander burned it in 330 BCE.

q: Which two superpowers led the opposing sides of the Cold War?
a: The United States and the Soviet Union
f: The rivalry lasted from the late 1940s to 1991 and was fought through proxy wars, spying and an arms race rather than direct war.

q: Which 1949 military alliance linked the U.S., Canada and Western European nations?
f: Its core promise, Article 5, says an attack on one member is an attack on all.

q: Which Soviet leader visited the United States in 1959 and later pulled missiles out of Cuba?
f: He led the USSR from 1953 to 1964 and denounced Stalin's crimes in 1956.

q: Which U.S. president demanded 'Tear down this wall' at the Berlin Wall in 1987?
f: He spoke at the Brandenburg Gate, and the wall fell in 1989.

q: What does 'detente' mean in Cold War diplomacy?
a: A relaxation of tensions between rivals
f: Detente marked the 1970s, with arms-control talks and the 1972 Nixon visits to Beijing and Moscow.

q: Which treaty, opened for signature in 1968, aims to stop the spread of nuclear weapons?
f: It recognizes five nuclear-weapon states and commits others not to acquire the bomb.

q: Which U.S. president visited Beijing in 1972 and met Mao Zedong?
f: The trip opened the way to normalized U.S.-China relations in 1979.

q: In which year did the Soviet Union dissolve?
f: The red flag came down over the Kremlin on December 25, 1991, and 15 republics became independent.

q: Which group carried out the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States?
f: The attacks led to the U.S. invasion of Afghanistan weeks later.

q: Which U.S. foreign-policy strategy aimed to stop the spread of communism?
f: George Kennan outlined the idea in 1946-47, and it guided U.S. policy for decades.

q: Which war saw the United States fight to keep North Vietnam's communists from taking over the south?
f: U.S. combat troops left in 1973, and Saigon fell in April 1975.

q: Which international organization, headquartered in New York, has 193 member states?
f: It was founded in 1945 with 51 members.

q: Which 1975 agreement recognized Europe's postwar borders and included human-rights commitments?
f: Signed by 35 states, it later gave dissidents in the Soviet bloc a tool to press for rights.

q: Which 1955 alliance bound the Soviet Union and its Eastern European allies?
f: It was dissolved in 1991.

q: Which 1945 conference saw Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin plan postwar Europe in Crimea?
f: It set the stage for the division of Germany and Europe's postwar order.

q: Which Egyptian president nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956?
f: Britain, France and Israel attacked, but U.S. and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw.

q: What did the U.S. call its 1962 naval action around Cuba, to avoid the legal term 'blockade'?
f: A blockade could be seen as an act of war, so Kennedy used the word 'quarantine'.

q: Which 1979 Soviet action led the U.S. to boycott the 1980 Moscow Olympics?
f: The war lasted until 1989.

q: Which Polish trade union led by Lech Walesa challenged communist rule in the 1980s?
f: It won Poland's partly free elections in 1989.

q: Which 1989 protests in Beijing were crushed by the Chinese government?
f: The crackdown began on the night of June 3-4, 1989.

q: Which U.S. spy plane was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960?
f: Pilot Francis Gary Powers was captured, wrecking a planned summit.

q: Soviet troops withdrew from which country in 1989 after nearly a decade of war?
f: The war cost the USSR roughly 15,000 lives and is often called its Vietnam.

q: Which U.S. secretary of state became famous for 'shuttle diplomacy' after the 1973 Arab-Israeli war?
f: He flew between Middle Eastern capitals to negotiate disengagement agreements.

q: Which 1990-91 conflict saw a U.S.-led coalition drive Iraq out of Kuwait?
f: The air campaign began in January 1991 and ground fighting lasted about 100 hours.

q: Which of these is NOT a permanent member of the UN Security Council?
f: The five permanent members, the U.S., U.K., France, Russia and China, hold veto power.

q: Which 1972 treaty limited U.S. and Soviet anti-ballistic missile systems?
f: The U.S. withdrew from it in 2002.

q: Which 1987 treaty eliminated an entire class of U.S. and Soviet missiles?
f: It banned ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 km; the U.S. left it in 2019.

q: Which 1956 uprising did Soviet tanks crush in Budapest?
f: Thousands died, and about 200,000 Hungarians fled.

q: Who led the 1968 'Prague Spring' reforms in Czechoslovakia?
f: His 'socialism with a human face' ended when Warsaw Pact forces invaded in August 1968.

q: Which failed 1961 U.S.-backed invasion targeted Cuba?
f: Cuban forces crushed the exile brigade in about three days.

q: Which 1964 resolution gave President Johnson broad powers to escalate in Vietnam?
f: It followed reported attacks on U.S. ships, one of which probably never happened.

q: Which 1953 coup, backed by the CIA and MI6, overthrew Iran's prime minister?
f: It restored the Shah's power, and its memory shaped Iranian views of the West.

q: Which 1992 treaty created the European Union?
f: It was signed in the Dutch city of Maastricht and took effect in 1993.

q: Which 1957 treaty created the European Economic Community?
f: Six countries signed it: France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

q: Which U.S. diplomat's 1946 'Long Telegram' laid the intellectual base for containment?
f: He wrote it from the U.S. embassy in Moscow.

q: Which leader hosted the 1955 Bandung Conference of Asian and African states as Indonesia's president?
f: It laid groundwork for the Non-Aligned Movement.

q: Which Yugoslav leader broke with Stalin in 1948 and helped found the Non-Aligned Movement?
f: Yugoslavia stayed communist but outside the Soviet bloc.

q: Which Soviet-bloc organization (1949-1991) coordinated economic ties among communist states?
f: It was the Soviet answer to the Marshall Plan.

q: Which 1983 NATO exercise alarmed Soviet leaders who feared it masked a real attack?
f: Historians still debate how close it came to causing a nuclear scare.

q: Which 1991 treaty cut U.S. and Soviet strategic nuclear arsenals?
f: Signed by Bush and Gorbachev just months before the USSR collapsed.

q: What is the 1960s rupture between Beijing and Moscow called?
f: It was ideological and territorial, and it led to border clashes in 1969.

q: Which two Asian giants fought a border war in 1962?
f: China declared a unilateral ceasefire after a month; the border remains disputed.

q: Which Czech dissident co-wrote Charter 77 and later became president?
f: He led the 1989 'Velvet Revolution' and served as president of Czechoslovakia and then Czechia.

q: Which of these countries was NEVER a member of the Warsaw Pact?
f: Tito's Yugoslavia stayed communist but non-aligned, and Albania left the pact in 1968.

q: Which of these was NOT one of NATO's twelve founding members in 1949?
f: Greece and Turkey joined in 1952.

q: Which Hungarian prime minister was executed in 1958 after the 1956 revolution?
f: He was reburied with honors in 1989, as communism ended.

q: Which Congolese leader was killed in 1961 amid Cold War intrigue?
f: He was the first prime minister of independent Congo.

q: Which 1973 action by Arab oil producers caused oil prices to roughly quadruple?
f: It targeted countries seen as backing Israel in the Yom Kippur War.

q: On which river did the 1969 Sino-Soviet border clashes occur?
f: The fighting centered on Zhenbao (Damansky) Island.

q: Which Ghanaian president championed Pan-Africanism and was ousted in 1966?
f: Ghana had been the first sub-Saharan colony to gain independence, in 1957.

q: Which 1990 treaty set limits on conventional forces in Europe?
f: It cut tanks, artillery and aircraft on both sides of the old Iron Curtain.

q: Which treaty allows unarmed surveillance flights over members' territory?
f: It was signed in 1992, but the U.S. and Russia later withdrew.

q: Which 1963 treaty banned nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and underwater?
f: Underground testing continued.

q: Which 1996 treaty bans all nuclear explosions but has still not entered into force?
f: It needs ratification by specific nuclear-capable states, including the U.S. and China.

q: Which 1994 agreement saw Ukraine give up Soviet nuclear weapons in exchange for security assurances?
f: Russia, the U.S. and the U.K. pledged to respect Ukraine's borders.

q: Which 1986 summit in Iceland nearly produced deep U.S.-Soviet nuclear cuts?
f: Reagan and Gorbachev came close to agreeing to abolish nuclear arsenals.
